When a protocol, API, or domain model uses `null`, `undefined`, and "empty" values (`""`, `[]`, `{}`) to mean different things — e.g. "no change" vs "explicit clear" vs "genuinely empty" — do not conflate them with loose comparisons, `??`, or spread/defaulting logic. Each sentinel must be handled on its own terms:

- At boundaries where data comes from an external or untrusted source (another process's JSON-RPC reply, a protobuf-decoded message, a stored record), narrow the value to the exact type you expect rather than trusting a type assertion. A pagination cursor typed as `string | undefined` but received as raw JSON can actually be `null`; checking `typeof value === "string"` before using it avoids an infinite loop that a naive `!== undefined` check lets through.
- Protobuf/JSON decoding often turns "field omitted" into a default (`""`, `[]`), not `undefined`. Code that does `images ?? retry.images` to "fall back when nothing was sent" will silently discard a real fallback when the wire format sends `[]` instead of `undefined`. Check for the actual empty-but-present case (`images?.length ? images : retry.images`) instead of relying on nullish coalescing alone.
- When `null` is a meaningful instruction (e.g. "clear this field") distinct from `undefined` ("leave it as is") and from an empty object/string (a real value), preserve that distinction end-to-end through serialization. Don't normalize `null` into `{}`/omitted or vice versa without checking what each encoding actually causes downstream.
- Treat "empty but present" (`[]`) and "absent" (`null`) as equivalent only when the domain genuinely doesn't distinguish them (e.g. an empty archive array should be treated the same as no archive) — and say so explicitly in the code/comment, rather than letting it fall out of incidental truthiness checks.
- If a defensive branch is reached only because a value that should never be null/missing turned out to be, fail loudly (throw) instead of silently falling through to normal-path logic that assumes the value is present — a silent fallthrough can re-trigger the exact bug the guard was meant to prevent.

Add a regression test for each such case, since these bugs reliably hide behind "the happy path never hits this."
